title: Rome’s three eras
description: Roman history runs from the Kingdom to the Republic (509 BCE) to the Empire (27 BCE); the West fell in 476 CE and the East in 1453.

facts.text: Roman tradition dated the founding of Rome to 753 BCE.
Roman history is usually divided into the Kingdom, the Republic (from 509 BCE) and the Empire (from 27 BCE).
The last emperor in the West, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed in 476 CE, the usual date given for the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
The eastern half of the empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until the city fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.

title: An empire around a sea
description: At its height Rome ruled every coast of the Mediterranean, which Romans called “our sea.”

facts.text: At its height the Roman Empire surrounded the Mediterranean, stretching from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the Middle East.
Romans called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.”

title: Romulus and Remus
description: Rome’s founding legend: twins raised by a she-wolf, a fratricide, and a city named for Romulus.

facts.text: According to legend, Rome was founded by the twins Romulus and Remus, sons of the god Mars, who were abandoned as babies and nursed by a she-wolf.
The she-wolf nursing the twins became one of Rome’s best-known symbols.
In the legend, Romulus killed Remus in a quarrel over the new city, which was named after Romulus.
Romans also traced their ancestry to Aeneas, a Trojan prince who, in legend, fled the fall of Troy to Italy.
Historians treat Rome’s founding stories as legend: they were written down centuries after the events they describe.

title: Rome’s first villages
description: Archaeology shows Latin hilltop villages from about the 8th century BCE that merged into a town around a drained valley, the Forum.

facts.text: The first Romans were Latins, a people of the region of Latium in central Italy.
Archaeologists have found traces of Iron Age huts on the Palatine Hill from around the 8th century BCE, close to the traditional founding date.
Early Rome grew from small hilltop villages that gradually merged into one community.
The valley that became the Roman Forum was once marshy and was drained, helped by the great drain later called the Cloaca Maxima.
Parts of the Cloaca Maxima still carry water today.

title: Seven hills and a river
description: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on defensible hills, with Ostia as its port.

facts.text: Rome grew where the Tiber River could be crossed, near an island in the river, about 25 km from the sea.
An ancient salt route, later called the Via Salaria, passed through Rome’s site, linking the coast with inland Italy.
Ancient Rome was built on seven hills beside the Tiber, among them the Palatine and the Capitoline.
The hills were easier to defend and stayed dry when the Tiber flooded the low ground between them.
Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, became Rome’s port, through which grain and other goods reached the city.

title: The Etruscans
description: Rome’s powerful northern neighbors, whose kings, symbols and rituals shaped early Rome.

facts.text: The Etruscans lived in Etruria, the region north of Rome in what is now Tuscany.
The Etruscans were organized in independent cities and were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy.
The Etruscan language is unrelated to Latin and is still only partly understood.
According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans.
The fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe carried before Roman officials as a sign of authority, came from the Etruscans.
Romans learned haruspicy, reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals, from the Etruscans.

title: The seven kings
description: Tradition counts seven kings from 753 to 509 BCE, chosen with the approval of the Senate and people.

facts.text: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud, ruling from 753 to 509 BCE.
Roman kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says each king was chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people.
Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and calendar.
Servius Tullius, the sixth king, was credited with the first census, which organized citizens by wealth.
The Roman Senate began as a council of elders advising the king.

title: Roman religion
description: Correct ritual kept the peace of the gods, from household spirits to Jupiter’s temple, Vesta’s fire and augury.

facts.text: Roman religion stressed performing rituals correctly; the aim was to keep the pax deorum, peace with the gods.
Roman households honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a household shrine.
Rome’s greatest temple, on the Capitoline Hill, was dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods, together with Juno and Minerva.
The Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, which was never allowed to go out.
Before major public decisions Romans consulted augurs, priests who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds; unfavorable signs could delay public business.

title: The Roman family
description: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants; the familia included the whole household.

facts.text: The paterfamilias, the oldest living male of a family, held legal power over his children and grandchildren, even as adults.
In early Roman law this power, patria potestas, in theory included the power of life and death over family members.
A Roman familia meant the whole household, including the enslaved people who lived and worked in it.
Noble Roman families kept wax masks of their ancestors and carried them in funeral processions.
A Roman man’s name usually had three parts, as in Gaius Julius Caesar: a personal name, a clan name and a family branch name.

title: The end of the kings
description: Tarquin the Proud was expelled in 509 BCE after the Lucretia scandal, and Romans swore never to have a king again.

facts.text: Tarquin the Proud, the seventh king, was remembered as a tyrant who ruled by force and ignored the Senate.
According to Roman tradition, the assault on the noblewoman Lucretia by the king’s son led to an uprising against the monarchy.
Led by Lucius Junius Brutus, the Romans expelled their king in 509 BCE and ended the monarchy.
Brutus had the Romans swear never again to allow anyone to be king in Rome.
Afterwards the title rex, king, was so hated in Rome that even its most powerful later leaders avoided it.

title: How Rome began
description: A strategic river site, merging Latin villages, Etruscan influence and founding legends together explain early Rome.

facts.text: Early Rome’s rise combined a strategic site on the Tiber, Latin villages that merged into a town, strong Etruscan influence, and founding legends Romans used to explain who they were.
